title: Three Narasimha Shrines of Sri Rangam
body:
When most people think of Sri Rangam, they think at once of the great temple of Sri Ranganātha, and rightly so, for it is vast, ancient and full of history. But in and around Sri Rangam there are also three small but powerful shrines of Lord Narasimha. They are not on the usual pilgrim's round, yet anyone who loves quiet places of strong spiritual presence will treasure a visit to them.

The first is Kāṭṭu Azhagiya Singar, which is believed to be older even than the temple of Sri Ranganātha. Kāṭṭu means forest, and in olden times this place was exactly that, a thick forest between the Kāveri and the Kollidam. Rishis lived and performed penance here, but wild animals, elephants above all, troubled them. Powerful as they were, the rishis did not wish to spend their strength in fighting them, and instead they prayed to Lord Narasimha. Moved by their devotion, the Lord appeared here and agreed to stay and protect them, and so He is called Kāṭṭu Azhagiya Singar, the beautiful lion-faced Lord of the forest.

The deity is believed to be svayambhu, self-manifested. He is seated, with Lakshmi Devī on His left thigh, and He faces west, which is rare. The shrine has no utsava vigraham of its own: because the temple once stood deep in an unsafe forest, its processional deity was kept in the Kūrattāzhwān sannidhi inside the temple of Sri Ranganātha, and so it is kept to this day. Once a year, on the evening of Vijayadashamī, Namperumāl, the utsavar of Sri Rangam, comes here in a grand procession. It is believed that the Goddess Lakshmi, performing penance here, hands Him a bow and arrow, and Namperumāl, on horseback, shoots an arrow at a vanni tree, signifying the victory of good over evil.

The second is Āṭṭru Azhagiya Singar, which is easy to miss unless one knows where to look. It stands near the bridge over the Kāveri that joins Chintāmaṇi and Tiruvānaikkāval: just before the bridge, one turns right towards the bypass road, and the shrine is a short way along on the left. Here Lord Narasimha sits with Lakshmi Devī on His lap, her hands folded towards Him in añjali, a touching depiction, and the shrine is much loved by those who pray for a good marriage. Originally Azhagiya Maṇavāḷa Perumāl was the presiding deity here, but when Lakshmi Narasimha came, He graciously gave up His place to Him and became the utsavar. There is also a beautiful Garuḍa vāhanam with Narasimha here, and the whole shrine has a warm and welcoming feel.

The third, Mettu Azhagiya Singar, is inside the temple of Sri Ranganātha itself, in the fifth prākāram near the northern gopuram, and it is bound up with the poet Kamban, the author of the Kamba Rāmāyaṇam. When Kamban came to present his Rāmāyaṇam at Sri Rangam, some of the āchāryas raised objections, chiefly because it described the Hiraṇya Samhāram, the slaying of Hiraṇyakashipu. Kamban humbly said, "Let us leave it to Perumāl," and prayed sincerely to Lord Narasimha. Suddenly a roar came from this sannidhi, as if the Lord Himself were giving His approval, and after that nobody said a word: Kamban's work was accepted. The spot is still called the Kambar Maṇḍapam, and opposite it is Mettu Azhagiya Singar, in a fierce form with eight arms, Hiraṇyakashipu on His lap and Prahlāda below His knee.

Each of these shrines is small beside the temple of Sri Ranganātha, yet each holds a great deal of soul. In the quiet protection of the forest Lord, in the grace that blesses marriages, and in the roar that upheld Kamban's devotion, Lord Narasimha reveals a different aspect of Himself. Whoever visits Sri Rangam should add these three shrines to their pilgrimage: there will be no crowds, but there will be peace, power and presence.
